p: Many software ideas die from the same cause: the first version tries to do everything. The team spends months on features, polish and edge cases, runs out of money or energy, and launches a product that nobody has validated. A minimum viable product, or MVP, is a deliberate way to avoid that trap.

This article explains what an MVP actually is, how to decide what goes into it and what stays out, how to test your idea cheaply before writing much code, and how to tell whether the launch worked. The examples are written for founders and business owners, not for engineers.

h: What an MVP is, and what it is not
p: An MVP is the smallest version of a product that lets real users complete the main task and lets you learn whether the idea is worth continuing. The important word is viable. It must genuinely solve the problem for the first users, even if it does so in a limited way.

It is not a broken prototype, a demo with fake buttons or a cheap version of the final product. A cheap product that frustrates users will teach you nothing except that people dislike frustrating products. It is also not a fixed list of features. Two companies building a booking tool might have very different MVPs, depending on who their first customers are.

A useful way to think about it is a skateboard before a car. The skateboard gets someone from A to B slowly. A wheel and a steering bar on their own do not. Each step should be something people can actually use.

h: Start with one problem and one type of user
p: The most common reason an MVP grows too big is that it serves too many people. Pick one type of user with one clear problem. A tool for every kind of restaurant becomes a tool for none. A tool that helps small catering businesses schedule deliveries is specific enough to design, build and test.

Write the problem in a sentence a customer would recognise: I lose time every morning turning emails into a delivery list. Then talk to at least a handful of people who have that problem. Ask how they handle it today, what it costs them and what they have already tried. If they have never tried to solve it, it may not be a painful enough problem.

Every idea rests on assumptions. Some are comfortable, such as people will use their phones. Others could sink the project: customers will pay for this, or restaurants will trust a stranger with their orders. List your assumptions and mark the ones that, if wrong, would make the whole product pointless.

Your MVP should be designed to test the riskiest assumption first. If the risk is that nobody will pay, a landing page with a price and a sign-up form can tell you more in two weeks than a finished app can in six months. If the risk is technical, such as whether you can import data from a certain system, build only that part first.

h: Choose features with a simple priority method
p: A practical method is to sort every feature idea into four groups. Must have: the product cannot do its main job without it. Should have: important but the product works without it. Could have: pleasant extras. Will not have this time: ideas you are consciously postponing.

Be strict with the must-have group. A useful test is to ask: if this feature were missing on launch day, would the first user still complete the main task? If yes, it is not a must-have. Login, the core action, and a way to see the result are usually must-haves. Dashboards, advanced settings and social sharing usually are not.
list: Write each feature as a user action, such as book an appointment, not as a technical component.
Score each feature for how much it helps the first user and how much effort it needs.
Build the high-help, low-effort items first and push the rest to later releases.

h: What to cut, and what you should never cut
p: Cutting features is healthy. Cutting basic quality is not. The following can usually wait: multiple languages, complex user roles, detailed analytics dashboards, custom themes, integrations with systems your first users do not use, and mobile apps if a responsive website will do.

Some things should never be cut, even in a small first version. Security basics such as hashed passwords, encrypted connections and proper access control protect your users and your reputation. Regular backups protect you from losing everything. A way for users to contact you protects the relationship. And basic measurement, such as knowing how many people sign up and complete the main task, is how you will learn anything at all.

h: Test before you build: fake it first
p: You can often validate demand with no software at all. In a concierge test, you deliver the service manually to a few customers while pretending the product exists, which reveals what they truly need. In a Wizard of Oz test, the interface looks automated but a person does the work behind the scenes.

You can also assemble a first version from existing tools: a form builder, a spreadsheet, an automation service and email. This is not embarrassing. Many successful products began as a form and a spreadsheet. Once the manual version is clearly useful and the work becomes repetitive, you have strong evidence for what to automate and a clear specification for the developers.

h: A worked example: a delivery scheduler for caterers
p: Suppose a founder wants to build software for small catering businesses. The riskiest assumption is that caterers will leave their email and spreadsheet habits and pay a monthly fee. Before building, the founder interviews eight caterers, and offers three of them a manual service: send orders by email and receive a clean delivery sheet each morning, prepared by hand.

Two of the three keep using it and ask for text alerts to drivers. That tells the founder the must-haves: capture orders, produce a daily delivery list, and notify drivers. Customer accounts, invoicing and reporting move to the later list. The first build is a simple web app with order entry, a daily list and SMS alerts. It launches with those three caterers, who are asked for weekly feedback.
Notice what happened: the build was small, informed by real behaviour, and aimed at the biggest risk. This is a fictional illustration, but the pattern is widely applicable.

h: Decide how you will know it worked
p: Before launch, agree on two or three success measures and a time frame. Good measures are behaviours, not opinions: the number of users who complete the main task in their first week, how many return in the following week, how many are willing to pay, and how many support requests relate to confusion about the main flow.

Avoid vanity numbers such as page views or downloads on their own. A hundred sign-ups who never come back is worse than ten who use the product every day. Write down in advance what result would make you continue, change direction or stop. It is much harder to be honest about this after months of work.

After launch, listen first and build second. Group feedback into patterns: what do several users ask for, what do they struggle with, and what do they ignore? Fix the biggest blockers in the main flow before adding new features. Watch real sessions if you can, or ask a few users to complete the main task while you observe silently.

Plan the code with growth in mind without over-engineering. A tidy, simple structure, automated tests for the most important flows and clear documentation make later changes cheaper. You do not need to design for a million users on day one, but you should avoid shortcuts that force a full rewrite at the first sign of success.

list: Building for everyone, which makes every decision harder and the product vaguer.
Treating the MVP as a throwaway and ignoring security, backups and basic quality.
Launching to friends and family only, whose praise is kind but not a reliable signal.
Adding features in response to every request instead of looking for patterns.
Having no success criteria, so that any result can be explained away.
Write the problem and the single type of user you are serving.
Interview at least five potential users about how they cope today.
List assumptions and pick the riskiest one to test first.
Run a manual or no-code test where possible.
Sort features into must, should, could and not now.
Define two or three success measures and a decision date.
Build only the must-haves, with security and backups included.
Launch to a small group, gather feedback weekly, and decide what to do next.

p: How much does an MVP cost? It depends on the scope and who builds it, so any single number would be misleading. The way to keep cost down is to limit the first release to one user type and one main task, and to test demand manually before building.
How long should an MVP take to build? Usually weeks rather than many months. If your plan stretches far beyond a few months, the scope is probably too large and can be split into smaller releases.

Should an MVP be a website, a mobile app or something else? Choose the simplest option your first users already use. For many business tools, a responsive web app reaches everyone on every device without app store approval, and can be turned into an app later if the need is proven.

What if the MVP fails? Then it did its job cheaply. You learned that the idea, the audience or the price was wrong before spending the full budget, and you can adjust or stop with most of your resources intact.

list: An MVP is the smallest product that really solves one problem for one type of user and teaches you something.
Test your riskiest assumption first, and consider a manual or no-code version before building.
Prioritise ruthlessly, but never skip security, backups and basic measurement.
Define success measures and a decision point before launch.
Use real user behaviour, not opinions, to decide what to build next.
